title: VMAC 2 coconut (makapuno): Characteristics
metaDescription: VMAC 2 coconut is a coconut variety from Visayas State University. See its days to harvest, yield, pest ratings, traits and where it grows best.
excerpt: VMAC 2 is a registered coconut variety, also sold or known as makapuno or makapuno hybrid 2. It was registered with the National Seed Industry Council in 2008 as NSIC 2008 Co 28. VSU bred it.

heroImage.alt: Tall coconut palms over a grassy field in Sipocot, Camarines Sur, the kind of farm where VMAC 2 coconut is grown

blocks.text: If you came here looking for makapuno or makapuno hybrid 2, this is the same coconut. Its seller and farm sources add notes, listed at the end. Compare it with the others in our [coconut variety finder](/crop-varieties/coconut), or see [every crop variety](/crop-varieties) we list. For the crop itself, read our guide: [coconut fertilizer by age](/crops/coconut-fertilizer).

blocks.caption: Key facts of VMAC 2
rows: about 144 nuts per palm a year

blocks.text: When does it bear, and how much?

A registered tree variety is described from its mother tree, not from trial plots. The mother tree of VMAC 2 was about 9 years old when it was registered. It bears all year, with fruit in 12. A grafted or marcotted tree bears years sooner than one grown from seed, and its yield climbs as the tree grows.

anee.io keeps the records of each block of trees, from fertilizer to harvest, with [the growth stages and weather](/features/growth-stages-and-weather) beside them.
Is it resistant to pests and diseases?
No pest or disease ratings are published for this variety. So treat it as untested, and scout every week.

The pests and diseases that hit coconut fields most often: [coconut bud rot](/diseases/coconut-bud-rot), [coconut cadang cadang](/diseases/cadang-cadang), [coconut leaf beetle (Brontispa)](/pests/coconut-leaf-beetle), [coconut rhinoceros beetle](/pests/coconut-rhinoceros-beetle), [coconut scale insect (cocolisap)](/pests/cocolisap). Our [pest finder](/pests) and [disease finder](/diseases) help you name what you see.

A fruit of VMAC 2 weighs about 1,690.31 g grams, and its shape is ovoid, angled. The edible part is 29.57 percent of the fruit. Its fruiting season is 12, bearing perennial. Each palm gave about 144 nuts a year in the records.
What its seller and farm sources say

items: **Yield:** About 144 nuts per palm a year.
**Fruit:** Nuts about 1.69 kg, makapuno meat about 1.7 cm thick.

blocks.text: Why farmers know it: vSU's second registered makapuno hybrid, with bigger nuts than VMAC 1. Check these against what farmers near you have seen, because the same variety can do differently from one town to the next.
Where and when to plant VMAC 2 coconut

Talls live long and stand typhoons, dwarfs bear early and are easy to harvest, and hybrids between the two give the most copra. Pick by use: copra, buko, or both. Get seednuts from a PCA accredited source. A registered tree variety is a selection from one proven mother tree, and only grafted, budded or marcotted plants carry its traits. A seedling grown from its seed can turn out quite different. So buy from a nursery accredited by the Bureau of Plant Industry, and ask which mother tree the scions came from. Before planting, get the field ready with our guide: [Land preparation for tree crops](/land-preparation/fruit-tree-land-preparation).

items: Buy grafted or budded plants from an accredited nursery, with the variety name on the tag.
Ask your municipal agriculturist or nearby farmers how it did in your area last season.
Plant a few trees first if the variety is new to your area, before you fill the whole farm.
Write down the planting day, inputs and harvest, so you can compare varieties on your own ground. anee.io keeps these records for you.

items.q: Is makapuno the same as VMAC 2?
items.a: Yes. makapuno is another name for VMAC 2, registered as NSIC 2008 Co 28. Seed sellers use both, so ask for either one.

items.q: Where can I buy planting material of VMAC 2?
items.a: Buy grafted, budded or marcotted trees from a nursery accredited by the Bureau of Plant Industry, so you get the true variety. Ask your provincial agriculture office for the nearest one.
